description: First reported in Puerto Rico, 1995, preceded by the 1975 'vampiro de Moca'. The name — 'chupa' (sucks) + 'cabra' (goat) = 'Goat-Sucker' — coined by Silverio Pérez. The Canóvanas sighting set the classic image: 4-5 feet, gray, wraparound eyes, spines. Types: bipedal reptilian kangaroo; quadrupedal hairless dog-like (mangy coyotes). Radford's 2011 study found predators and disease, not a vampire.
source: Puerto Rican/Latin American folklore — the Chupacabra goat-sucker cryptid documented since the 1990s.
research_notes: Condensed 1316→398. Kept 1995 Puerto Rico origin, Moca 1975 predecessor, name etymology + Silverio Perez, Canovanas classic image, two types with mangy-coyote resolution, Radford 2011 debunk.

description: The Feathered Serpent, key Mexican-American deity. Aztec god of wind (Ehecatl) and the morning star (Venus), he made humanity in Mictlan from his blood and ancestral bones. His name: 'quetzal' (green bird) + 'coatl' (serpent). Tricked by Tezcatlipoca into drunken incest, exiled, he vowed return from the east — a return conflated with Cortés's 1519 arrival. A Chicano symbol of indigenous identity.
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex
research_notes: Condensed 1240→399. Kept name etymology, Ehecatl/Venus domains, Mictlan creation from blood and bones, Tezcatlipoca trick, Cortes 1519 conflation, Chicano reclaiming.

description: Tusse (also Tuss): a troll/vätte variant of Halland, Småland, and Västergötland. A shaggy trickster that leads travelers astray — 'tussen har lett honom vilse' — it is more mischievous than evil, unlike the malevolent Puke. It repays porridge offerings: a bowl under a 'tusse-sten'; if eaten, the farm was protected, if not, trouble. The name survives in place names, from Old Norse þurs (giant).
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.
research_notes: Condensed 1280→396. Kept regional distribution, trickster behavior + Swedish saying, Puke contrast, porridge/tusse-sten custom, Old Norse þurs etymology; removed trailing filler line.

description: In Bhutan the black-necked crane (Grus nigricollis) is the soul of monks and nuns. Each October they circle Gangteng Monastery in the Phobjikha Valley three times clockwise — a Buddhist kora. The Sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso (1683–1706): 'Oh white crane, lend me your wings.' Killing a crane means life imprisonment, the harshest penalty in Bhutan. The November 11 festival marks their return.
source: RSPN Bhutan, Bhutanese folk traditions, Black-Necked Crane Festival records
research_notes: Condensed 1531→399. Kept reincarnation belief, Gangteng/Phobjikha kora, Dalai Lama verse, life-imprisonment protection, festival.

description: An obscure yokai said to haunt old wooden houses. The name pairs 'botamochi' (a spring-equinox sweet rice cake) with 'bakemono' ('transforming thing'). It lives under the floorboards, mimicking human voices to confuse, frighten, or amuse — imitating family at night. Unlike malevolent oni or yurei, it is a harmless prankster, among 'house yokai' like the Zashiki-warashi and Makura-kashi.
source: Japanese folklore; a yokai that mimics voices from under floorboards.
research_notes: Condensed 1157→389. Kept name etymology (botamochi rice cake, bakemono), floorboard voice mimicry, nocturnal pranks, house-yokai class.

description: Female Slavic nature spirit of Polish folklore, of forests, fields, lakes, rivers. The name from 'bóg' (god) marks these as minor nature goddesses. Boginki are beautiful enchantresses or hideous hags — broader than the Rusalki (drowned-maiden spirits). They guard wildlife, punishing sport hunting, plant theft, and disrespect; to the respectful they grant fertility, harvests, or protection.
source: Polish folklore — Boginka spirit documented in Polish oral tradition.
research_notes: Condensed 1015→392. Kept bóg etymology, dual beauty/hag form, Rusalki contrast, nature-protection role, benevolence to the respectful.

description: Powerful forest and swamp spirit of Polish mythology, tutelary of central and eastern Poland's woodlands — the Puszcza Kurpiowska. Unlike the Leshy, Boruta is a nobleman (szlachcic) who pacted with dark forces and haunts the forests; his name derives from Old Polish 'bor' (pine forest). He leads astray hunters, illegal loggers, and mushroom pickers, yet guides lost children home.
source: Polish folklore — Boruta is a forest spirit documented in Polish oral tradition.
research_notes: Condensed 1059→382. Kept Leshy comparison, szlachcic pact origin, bor etymology, Puszcza Kurpiowska, trickster/punisher duality and helpful side.
